We use a gamified decisionmaking task (Sookud et al., 2026) in which participants are presented with two temporally and perceptually distinct environments, enabling current and prior environmental volatility to be manipulated factorially, to establish how exposure to a prior environment affects learning in the current setting.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Following our preregistration, we aimed to recruit 400 participants in total, equally and randomly allocated to 4 versions of an online gamified cognitive task followed by six post-task questionnaires. The sample size was informed by an a priori power calculation based on pilot data, using a t-test comparing learning rates between two second stable blocks from the task (i.e., the stable-to-stable and volatile-to-stable conditions). The observed effect size (d=0.43) indicated that 86 participants per group were required to achieve 80% power. Accordingly, a target of 100 participants for each task condition was set to allow for exclusions while maintaining adequate power. Due to an error during recruitment two versions of the task included 101 participants. Following exclusions, the final sample size for the cognitive task was 330 participants.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Modelling Generalisation of Belief Updating
table.research_questions:
Our primary research questions and corresponding hypotheses are as follows:

Q1) How do learning styles generalise across different environments with varying uncertainty?  

Hypothesis  (H1): Prior block effects and computational learning parameters
Learning rate, estimated using a Rescorla-Wagner model fitted to participants’ choice behaviour and associated reward outcomes, will differ between blocks in each task version. Specifically, learning rates in the second block will reflect carryover effects from the first block, indicating generalisation of learning styles across environmental contexts. Based on pilot experiments, we expect this effect to be specific to stable environments (i.e., stable environments will be affected by prior experience), although we will also test for effects in volatile blocks as additional exploratory analyses.
 
Q2) Does trait anxiety influence the extent to which learning styles generalise across different environments? 

Hypothesis 2 (H2): Exploratory analyses of trait anxiety
Trait anxiety (STICSA scores) will be examined as a continuous predictor of computational indices of generalisation (i.e., difference in learning rates) across blocks for each task version. Although these analyses are exploratory, based on prior literature we expect trait anxiety level to be a significant predictor of learning rate changes across task blocks.
table.foreknowledge_of_data_or_evidence: Data does not yet exist. No part of the data that will be used for this analysis plan exists, and no part will be generated until after this plan is registered.

table.study_design_overview:
Each participant is randomly assigned to complete 1 out of 4 versions of a online gamified cognitive task (the cannonball task), which is in essence a 2-armed bandit. In this task, participants are asked to choose between two stimuli (a left or right cannon), each of which are predictive of reward (a cannonball that makes it to its target without exploding) to some extent, to earn as many points as possible. This is repeated for multiple different combinations of pairs of stimuli, and therefore involves trial-and-error learning. 

Version 1 of the task begins with a volatile block of 120 trials, in which the reward probability associated with one of two cannons switches every 20 trials. This is followed by a stable block of 120 trials, where the reward probability switches every 60 trials. To ensure participants perceive a significant change in environmental context, they are shown the message “You have now entered a new environment” before entering the second block, which has a visually distinct layout from the first block. 

Version 2 of the task uses the same statistical structure but reverses the order, starting with the stable block followed by the volatile block. Counterbalancing the order of these blocks/environmental contexts allows us to manipulate participants’ initial prior beliefs and examine how these priors generalise when environmental statistics change. However, despite such counterbalancing, participants will only complete one version of the task, as completing both would introduce substantial carry over effects (i.e., learning from the first task version would bias performance in the second).  

As control conditions, version 3 of the task begins with a volatile block of 120 trials followed by another volatile block of 120 trials, while version 4 begins with a stable block of 120 trials followed by another stable block of 120 trials. This ensures that the effects observed in versions 1 and 2 of the task can be attributed to changes in environmental volatility and block order. 

Once participants complete the task they are instructed to complete a series of six questionnaires online, assessing relevant psychological traits of interest, including: 

- Sate-Trait Inventory of Cognitive and Somatic Anxiety (STICSA): This will be used to measure trait anxiety. 
- Intolerance to Uncertainty Scale-12 (IUS-12): This will be used to assess sensitivity to uncertainty (and compared to individuals’ task performance).
- Patient Health Questionnaire 8 item (PHQ-8): This will be used to control for high depressive symptoms.
- Generalised Anxiety Disorder 7 item scale (GAD-7): This will be used to control for high depressive symptoms. 
- Revised Life Oriented Test (LOT-R): This will be used to measure general expectations about positive and negative outcomes. 
- Transdiagnostic symptoms inventory (Hopkins et al., 2022): This will be used as a brief measure of additional transdiagnostic mental health symptoms. 

Scores obtained from these questionnaires will allow us to identify the extent to which anxiety scores (individuals with lower- vs higher-trait anxiety) influence task performance (generalisation effects), while accounting for other mental health characteristics. 

Consequently, this study uses a mixed factorial design. Task version is manipulated between subjects, such that each participant completes only one version of the cannonball task (versions 1-4), while environmental context (volatile vs. stable blocks) is manipulated within subjects, allowing behaviour to be compared across contexts within each task version. Additionally, trait anxiety is not treated as a categorical grouping variable but instead measured continuously and incorporated into regression analyses. Specifically, individual anxiety scores (from the STICSA questionnaire) are used to predict learning-related parameters (i.e., Learning Rate) estimated from task performance, to examine if and how anxiety modulates behavioural adaptation and generalisation across environmental contexts. Together, the combination of these between- and within-subject components constitute a mixed factorial design. 

Following the behavioural analysis of participants’ learning patterns across environmental contexts, a computational model based on the Rescorla-Wagner framework and Hierarchical Bayesian modelling will be applied to the task data. This model will be used to estimate key learning parameters, including learning rate, with the aim of reproducing the belief updating patterns observed from participants’ behaviour/performance in the task. Since both the task and computational model rely on model-free learning (i.e., learning through trial and error), this allows us to effectively observe how prior belief updating evolves over time and across environmental contexts (aligning with our aims and hypotheses).
table.data_collection_procedures: Participants will be recruited through the online platform Prolific, which allows access to a large and diverse participant pool. Broad inclusion criteria will be applied in the aim of obtaining a representative sample. Specifically, eligible participants must be based in the UK, aged 18 or older to ensure informed consent can be provided, and must have an acceptance rate of >=98% on Prolific, indicating a history of reliable, high-quality responses and ensuring data integrity. No additional exclusion criteria will be applied.
table.sample_size: Based on pilot data and power analyses, we aim to recruit up to 100 participants per task version. However, because participants who fail to complete all trials or show evidence of inattentive responding (i.e., random responding on >=75% of trials) will be excluded from statistical analyses, the final sample sizes across task versions/conditions are not expected to be equal, but anticipated to fall within the range of approximately 90-100 participants for each task version.
table.sample_size_rationale: The sample size is based on a power calculation using effect sizes from a pilot study based on a t-test on learning rates between the two second stable blocks (i.e., from the stable > stable and volatile > stable conditions), where an effect size of d=0.43 indicates that 86 participants in each group are required for 80% power. Our target of 100 per group allows for exclusions, and we also include 100 participants for all conditions to allow testing of effects on volatile blocks (although strong effects were not observed here in piloting).
table.stopping_rule:
Data collected during pilot testing will not be included in the analyses reported in this study. Formal data collection for the study will begin once the finalised task is deployed and participant recruitment begins via Prolific. 

Data collection will terminate once 100 participants per task version have been obtained.
table.manipulated_variables:
The independent variables in the current study include trait anxiety score, task version, and environmental context. Specifically, trait anxiety is measured using each participants' STICSA post-task questionnaire scores and is treated as a continuous individual-difference variable. These scores are incorporated into between-subject regression analyses to examine how variation in trait anxiety relates to task performance. 

Task version is a between-subjects factor, with participants completing either Version 1 (volatile-to-stable), Version 2 (stable-to-volatile), Version 3 (volatile-to-volatile), or Version 4 (stable-to-stable) of the adapted cannonball task. In contrast, environmental context is a within-subjects factor, as all participants experience both volatile and stable blocks within their assigned task version, allowing us to examine the effects of each block on participants’ performance.

With regards to the computational model, the independent variables include task version and environmental context, as these define the statical structure of the learning environment and drive belief updating. Trait anxiety, however, is not modelled as an independent variable within the model itself; instead, it is treated as a continuous individual-difference measure and used in regression analyses of the model’s estimated parameters (learning rate) to assess whether variation in anxiety modulates learning dynamics.

These independent variables allow us to investigate how individual differences in anxiety and the type of environmental statistics influence learning, belief updating, and generalisation (the primary dependent variables). 

However, although the primary focus is on comparing low- to high-trait anxious individuals and their distinct belief updating patterns, participants with elevated depression scores (from post-task questionnaires) will not be excluded from the study. Including these participants allows us to account for variance associated with depressive symptoms while isolating trait anxiety-specific effects on belief updating. Incorporating depression as a covariate therefore controls for potential confounding effects, ensuring that observed differences can be confidently attributed to trait anxiety.
table.measured_variables:
The primary dependent variables in this study are derived from participants’ performance in the adapted cannonball task, specifically choice behaviour as well as the trial outcome (i.e., if the cannonball exploded or not for a given choice) for training the computational model. Our primary measure is the degree of generalisation between environmental contexts (e.g., volatile-to-stable vs. stable-to-volatile blocks) as estimated based on the learning rate parameter from a Rescorla-Wagner model, including learning rate. 

We will also run exploratory analyses using other computational models (e.g., dual learning rate models or Pearce-Hall models), and may also look at metrics derived from choice behaviour directly (e.g., choice variability).
table.indices: Computational indices are derived by fitting a Rescorla–Wagner model (using hierarchical Bayesian modelling) to participants’ trial-by-trial choice behaviour and outcome data (i.e., whether the cannonball exploded or not on a given trial). The primary model-derived parameter of interest is the learning rate (α), which is estimated separately for each environmental context within each task version.
table.statistical_tests:
For computational modelling analyses, learning rates (α) are estimated independently for each block within each task version using the Rescorla-Wagner model. To address our primary research questions, participants’ behavioural data including choice (trial-by-trial switching) will be statistically analysed ANOVAs and t-tests. Between-subject ANOVAs will be conducted to compare choice behaviour across each task version. Therefore, Hypothesis 1 (H1) will be tested by assessing whether first-block performance predicts second-block performance, and therefore whether learning in the initial environment generalises to the subsequent environment. To achieve this, an ANOVA will be specified that uses data from only the 2nd blocks, with prior and current block type (as well as their interaction) as independent variables. H1 will be tested by 1) examining the main effect of prior block on learning rates, and 2) via a t-test comparing learning rates in the two 2nd stable blocks, given that we expect the effect to be specific to stable environments.

These analyses directly address H1 and H2 by testing whether learning rates generalise across environmental contexts (e.g., from the first to the second block) and whether this generalisation differs as a function of block order and environmental structure.  

Finally, to examine the relationship between learning dynamics and trait anxiety (H3), Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression analyses will be conducted with difference in learning rates between 1st and 2nd blocks as the dependent variable and STICSA scores as a continuous predictor variable. These regression analyses will be performed separately for each task version to assess whether individual differences in anxiety predict variation in learning rates across environmental contexts. Together, these analyses allow us to assess both the generalisation of learning across environments (H1) and the extent to which trait anxiety modulates learning dynamics (H2).
table.transformations: Learning rates will be subject to a logit transform for analyses using this variable as the dependent variable.
table.inference_criteria: Statistical significance for all ANOVAs, t-tests, and regression analyses will be evaluated using a two-tailed criteria of <0.05. Effect sizes will be reported using partial η² for ANOVAs, Cohen’s d for t-tests, and standardised regression coefficients for OLS analyses.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Participants who fail to complete all trials of the task or questions from post-task questionnaires we be excluded from analyses. Additionally, participants who show evidence of inattentive responding in the task or failing more than 1 infrequency item in the questionnaires (where the 1st and 2nd most "correct" answers are treated as correct) will be excluded.

Inattentive task behaviour will be determined as 1) selecting one option on >= 75% of trials, given that across the task both options are equally as rewarding, and 2) exhibiting low-variance responding (assessed by having a standard deviation of a 10-trial choice moving average of < 0.2, reflective of little learning).
table.missing_data_handling: Any missing data from participants will result in the given participant being removed from the data when carrying out analyses.

table.text: As expected, an ANOVA revealed that current block volatility (F(1, 326) = 10.04, p = .002, ηp² = .03) had a significant positive effect on learning rate derived from the Rescorla-Wagner learning model, such that learning rates were higher when participants were currently in a volatile environment.

table.text: However, and in line with our hypothesis, we also observed a significant effect of previous block volatility (F(1, 326) = 7.72, p = .006, ηp² = .02, Figure 3), indicating that learning rates were higher when participants had previously experienced a volatile environment.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .055", "p = 1.00", "p≥0.05", "p>0.05" ), Sentence = c("The interaction between current and previous block volatility was not significant (F(1, 326) = 3.70, p = .055, ηp² = .01), indicating that there was no clear evidence of a difference between stable and volatile current environments in the effect of previous volatility.", "Follow-up t-tests also revealed that this effect was most prominent in the current volatile condition (t(160) = -3.81, corrected p < .001, d = 0.60), while no significant difference was found when comparing conditions where the current block was stable (t(166) = 0.57, corrected p = 1.00, d = 0.09).", "Results indicated that trait anxiety, as well as all other mental health measures, did not significantly predict single or dual learning rate changes after applying FDR correction (p≥0.05).", "Regression analyses using these factor scores revealed that none of the four-factor solutions significantly predicted single or dual learning rate change in any of the task versions after applying FDR correction (p>0.05; Tables S9-S10)." )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. table.text: As expected, an ANOVA revealed that current block volatility (F(1, 326) = 10.04, p = .002, ηp² = .03) had a significant positive effect on learning rate derived from the Rescorla-Wagner learning model, such that learning rates were higher when participants were currently in a volatile environment.
table.eta_coherence_note: Match under partial eta-squared formula from F and dfs.

table.text: However, and in line with our hypothesis, we also observed a significant effect of previous block volatility (F(1, 326) = 7.72, p = .006, ηp² = .02, Figure 3), indicating that learning rates were higher when participants had previously experienced a volatile environment.
table.eta_coherence_note: Match under partial eta-squared formula from F and dfs.

table.text: The interaction between current and previous block volatility was not significant (F(1, 326) = 3.70, p = .055, ηp² = .01), indicating that there was no clear evidence of a difference between stable and volatile current environments in the effect of previous volatility.
table.eta_coherence_note: Match under partial eta-squared formula from F and dfs.

table.text: Follow-up t-tests also revealed that this effect was most prominent in the current volatile condition (t(160) = -3.81, corrected p < .001, d = 0.60), while no significant difference was found when comparing conditions where the current block was stable (t(166) = 0.57, corrected p = 1.00, d = 0.09).
table.d_coherence_note: Match under independent-samples equal-n assumption (n1 = n2 = 81, N = 162).

table.text: Follow-up t-tests also revealed that this effect was most prominent in the current volatile condition (t(160) = -3.81, corrected p < .001, d = 0.60), while no significant difference was found when comparing conditions where the current block was stable (t(166) = 0.57, corrected p = 1.00, d = 0.09).
table.d_coherence_note: Match under independent-samples equal-n assumption (n1 = n2 = 84, N = 168).

For t-tests with a reported d, coherence checks yielded 2 matches under assumptions.
For F-tests with a reported eta-squared effect size, coherence checks yielded 3 matches under assumptions.

codebook_check.title: Codebook Check
codebook_check.summary_text:
-  We parsed 33 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
-  0 of 266 data columns (0%) are documented in a codebook; 266 are not.
-  A codebook was found and parsed (33 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents ``min`, `max``, ``prior_mu_mean`, `prior_mu_sigma``, ``prior_sigma_scale`` while the data has `questionnaire_key`, `question_id`, `item_label`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.
report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.
We examined 5 codebook/README/label sources and 266 data columns across 27 files.

**A codebook was found and parsed (33 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents ``min`, `max``, ``prior_mu_mean`, `prior_mu_sigma``, ``prior_sigma_scale`` while the data has `questionnaire_key`, `question_id`, `item_label`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.**

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 266 columns across 27 data files.
#### Issues Identified
2 file/column combinations have at least one issue.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 27 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: We use a gamified decisionmaking task (Sookud et al., 2026) in which participants are presented with two temporally and perceptually distinct environments, enabling current and prior environmental volatility to be manipulated factorially, to establish how exposure to a prior environment affects learning in the current setting.
All participants were recruited via the online platform Prolific.
Eligible participants were those who were based in the UK, aged 18 or older to ensure informed consent could be provided, and had an acceptance rate of >=98% on Prolific.
All participants were compensated for their time at a rate of £9 per hour for completion of the study.
Participants were instructed to choose between two cannon-ball containers, each associated with a reward probability that varied across the task.
Participants were also required to aim at the alien, although this behaviour was only included as part of the cover story.
Participants completed only one task version to avoid carry-over effects between conditions.

Since we were interested in how learning rates generalise across distinct contexts, participants were presented with the message "You have now entered a new environment" before entering the second block, which had a visually distinct layout from the first block (see Figure 1), ensuring that participants perceived a significant change in the environmental context.

Once participants completed the task, they were asked to provide basic demographic information (age and sex), followed by a series of six questionnaires assessing common mental health problems, related symptoms, and personality traits: State-Trait Inventory of Cognitive and Somatic Anxiety (STICSA) (Boyer & Rodieck, 2017; Grös et al., 2007), Intolerance to Uncertainty Scale-12 (IUS-12) (Carleton et al., 2007), Patient Health Questionnaire 8 item (PHQ-8) (Spitzer et al., 1999), Generalised Anxiety Disorder 7 item scale (GAD-7) (Spitzer et al., 2006), Revised Life Oriented Test (LOT-R) (Scheier et al., 1994), and Transdiagnostic symptoms inventory (Hopkins et al., 2022).

Participants were excluded for inattentive task behaviour if they 1) selected one cannon on >=75% of trials, given that both options are equally rewarding across the task, or 2) exhibited a standard deviation of a 10-trial choice moving average of <0.2 (low-variance responding).
We recruited a sample of 402 participants.

As expected, an ANOVA revealed that current block volatility (F(1, 326) = 10.04, p = .002, ηp² = .03) had a significant positive effect on learning rate derived from the Rescorla-Wagner learning model, such that learning rates were higher when participants were currently in a volatile environment.

However, and in line with our hypothesis, we also observed a significant effect of previous block volatility (F(1, 326) = 7.72, p = .006, ηp² = .02, Figure 3), indicating that learning rates were higher when participants had previously experienced a volatile environment.
Each participant completed one of four versions, each providing a unique combination of stable and volatile conditions across the two blocks.

text.text: Humans are adept at learning under uncertainty.

However, the way in which we learn must adapt to different environments, and we must determine when to generalise learning strategies across different contexts, making use of prior experience to guide present learning.
However, how learning adapts based on prior experience remains poorly understood.
Here, we examine how prior exposure to environments with differing levels of uncertainty shapes subsequent learning.

A large sample recruited online (N=330) completed a gamified two-armed bandit task comprising two blocks with varying uncertainty, manipulated through the volatility or changeability of outcome contingencies.
Computational modelling enabled the extraction of learning rate parameters quantifying the speed with which participants update their expectations.

Analyses revealed significant effects of both previously experienced and current block volatility learning rates, and that this combination of generalisation and adaptation was consistent across learning from positive and negative prediction errors.
Exploratory regression and factor analyses did not identify any moderating effects of mental health symptoms.

Our results demonstrate that prior experience biases belief updating strategies across environments, revealing a mechanism through which learning both adapts and generalises to facilitate effective behaviour.
Updating of beliefs in response to new information is fundamental for adaptive learning and decision-making.
Prior beliefs represent our internal, pre-existing assumptions and expectations about the environment that inform how we interpret new information.

However, determining the appropriate balance between persisting with existing beliefs versus updating expectations according to new information is a challenge that humans must solve when facing dynamic and uncertain environments (Behrens et al., 2007).
text.formatted: However, determining the appropriate balance between persisting with existing beliefs versus updating expectations according to new information is a challenge that humans must solve when facing dynamic and uncertain environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Behrens et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Human learning is thought to be driven by prediction errors, representing mismatches between expectations and outcomes (Kube & Rozenkrantz, 2021).
text.formatted: Human learning is thought to be driven by prediction errors, representing mismatches between expectations and outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Kube & Rozenkrantz, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In reinforcement learning (RL) models, such as the Rescorla-Wagner model (Rescorla & Wagner, 1972; Sutton & Barto, 2018), the learning rate parameter governs how quickly these beliefs or expectations are updated after experiencing a prediction error.
text.formatted: In reinforcement learning (RL) models, such as the Rescorla-Wagner model <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Rescorla & Wagner, 1972;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Sutton & Barto, 2018)</ref>, the learning rate parameter governs how quickly these beliefs or expectations are updated after experiencing a prediction error.

text.text: Higher learning rates place greater weight on recent outcomes, indicating more rapid belief updating in response to immediate or recent feedback, while lower learning rates can result in adopting more conservative learning styles as it places more weight on previously established beliefs, indicating slower belief updating (Kandroodi et al., 2021; Rescorla & Wagner, 1972; Sutton & Barto, 2018).
text.formatted: Higher learning rates place greater weight on recent outcomes, indicating more rapid belief updating in response to immediate or recent feedback, while lower learning rates can result in adopting more conservative learning styles as it places more weight on previously established beliefs, indicating slower belief updating <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Kandroodi et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Rescorla & Wagner, 1972;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Sutton & Barto, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, how humans determine the optimal learning rate in any given environment remains an open question.
Using simple reward-learning tasks, environmental statistics can be manipulated to observe learning rates adjust accordingly.

For example, using a probability-tracking task, Behrens et al. (2007) demonstrated that participants adjust learning rates according to environmental volatility, the rate at which stimulus-outcome associations change.
text.formatted: For example, using a probability-tracking task, <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Behrens et al. (2007)</ref> demonstrated that participants adjust learning rates according to environmental volatility, the rate at which stimulus-outcome associations change.

text.text: Specifically, in volatile environments, where stimulus-outcome contingencies change frequently, people tend to rely more on recent outcomes, while in stable environments adopt more conservative learning styles when updating beliefs (Behrens et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Specifically, in volatile environments, where stimulus-outcome contingencies change frequently, people tend to rely more on recent outcomes, while in stable environments adopt more conservative learning styles when updating beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Behrens et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: These findings, alongside a number of others (McGuire et al., 2014; Nassar et al., 2010; Piray & Daw, 2021), suggest that adaptive learning involves using higher-order information about environmental statistics to distinguish meaningful changes in contingencies from less informative fluctuations.
text.formatted: These findings, alongside a number of others <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(McGuire et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Nassar et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Piray & Daw, 2021)</ref>, suggest that adaptive learning involves using higher-order information about environmental statistics to distinguish meaningful changes in contingencies from less informative fluctuations.

text.text: More broadly, establishing how humans determine how to learn (i.e., meta-learning) has assumed particular importance given interest in developing similarly flexible artificially intelligent systems (Wang et al., 2018; Wang, 2021; Khadse et al., 2025).
text.formatted: More broadly, establishing how humans determine how to learn (i.e., meta-learning) has assumed particular importance given interest in developing similarly flexible artificially intelligent systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Wang et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Wang, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Khadse et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Prior experience may also shape learning rate calibration by providing an informed starting point when entering a new environment.

Consistent with this hypothesis, Simoens et al. (2024) demonstrated that participants learned environment-specific reward learning rates in two environments following repeated encounters with each, findings which were replicated and extended by Simoens et al. (2026).
text.formatted: Consistent with this hypothesis, <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Simoens et al. (2024)</ref> demonstrated that participants learned environment-specific reward learning rates in two environments following repeated encounters with each, findings which were replicated and extended by <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Simoens et al. (2026)</ref>.

text.text: In real world scenarios, however, environments may not be continuously intermixed as in these previous studies.
Rather, agents may transition been distinct and temporally separable but persistent contexts, each requiring a particular learning rate.
For example, a student starting at a new school may need to determine whether to generalize prior experience or recalibrate in accordance with the new social environment.

Prior work demonstrates similar carry-over of volatility in task-rule learning, in that exposure to high versus low volatility influenced learning rates in a subsequent medium-volatility environment (Wen et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Prior work demonstrates similar carry-over of volatility in task-rule learning, in that exposure to high versus low volatility influenced learning rates in a subsequent medium-volatility environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Wen et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, it remains unclear whether reward-guided learning is similarly sensitive to prior experience, and substantial evidence indicates that learning rates are highly adaptable based on experienced outcomes (Behrens et al., 2007).
text.formatted: However, it remains unclear whether reward-guided learning is similarly sensitive to prior experience, and substantial evidence indicates that learning rates are highly adaptable based on experienced outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Behrens et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Besides the fundamental question regarding how learning rates adapt to distinct environments, computational psychiatry suggests that anxiety disorders are characterized by altered learning rate adaptation (Browning et al., 2015) and uncertainty estimation (Gibbs-Dean et al., 2023; Hein et al., 2021; Pulcu & Browning, 2019; Wise & Dolan, 2020), while generalization across experiences has also been implicated in anxiety (Verra et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Besides the fundamental question regarding how learning rates adapt to distinct environments, computational psychiatry suggests that anxiety disorders are characterized by altered learning rate adaptation <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Browning et al., 2015)</ref> and uncertainty estimation <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Gibbs-Dean et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Hein et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Pulcu & Browning, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Wise & Dolan, 2020)</ref>, while generalization across experiences has also been implicated in anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Verra et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: As such, it is pertinent to ask whether learning rate adaptation and generalization may be linked to symptoms of mental health problems such as anxiety disorders.
Here, we seek to establish how learning rates adapt across distinct environments, quantifying the influence of prior experience on learning within novel contexts.

We use a gamified decisionmaking task (Sookud et al., 2026) in which participants are presented with two temporally and perceptually distinct environments, enabling current and prior environmental volatility to be manipulated factorially, to establish how exposure to a prior environment affects learning in the current setting.
text.formatted: We use a gamified decisionmaking task <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Sookud et al., 2026)</ref> in which participants are presented with two temporally and perceptually distinct environments, enabling current and prior environmental volatility to be manipulated factorially, to establish how exposure to a prior environment affects learning in the current setting.

text.text: Using computational modelling, we demonstrate that learning rates are influenced by both the current environment's volatility and the volatility of the previously experienced environment, indicating that learning rates generalise across otherwise distinct environments.
We further explore how these processes relate to self-reported symptoms of mood and anxiety disorders.
This study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/9agzn).
text.formatted: This study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/9agzn">https://osf.io/9agzn</ref>).

text.text: Following our preregistration, we aimed to recruit 400 participants in total, equally and randomly allocated to 4 versions of an online gamified cognitive task followed by six post-task questionnaires.

The sample size was informed by an a priori power calculation based on pilot data, using a t-test comparing learning rates between two second stable blocks from the task (i.e., the stable-to-stable and volatile-to-stable conditions).
The observed effect size (d=0.43) indicated that 86 participants per group were required to achieve 80% power.
Accordingly, a target of 100 participants for each task condition was set to allow for exclusions while maintaining adequate power.
Due to an error during recruitment two versions of the task included 101 participants.
Following exclusions, the final sample size for the cognitive task was 330 participants.
All participants were recruited via the online platform Prolific.
Eligible participants were those who were based in the UK, aged 18 or older to ensure informed consent could be provided, and had an acceptance rate of >=98% on Prolific.
text.formatted: Eligible participants were those who were based in the UK, aged 18 or older to ensure informed consent could be provided, and had an acceptance rate of >=98% on Prolific.

text.text: All participants were compensated for their time at a rate of £9 per hour for completion of the study.
This study was ethically approved by the King's College London Research Ethics Committee (LRU/RGO-25/26-52823).
Each participant was randomly assigned to one of four versions of the online gamified cognitive task, referred to as the cannon ball task (adapted from Donegan et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Each participant was randomly assigned to one of four versions of the online gamified cognitive task, referred to as the cannon ball task (adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Donegan et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This represented a gamified version of 2-armed bandit problem with the primary objective of maximising the total number of points earned, as in previous tasks (Behrens et al., 2007; Browning et al., 2015; Simoens et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This represented a gamified version of 2-armed bandit problem with the primary objective of maximising the total number of points earned, as in previous tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Behrens et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Browning et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Simoens et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The task comprised of 240 trials (two blocks of 120 trials) in total, with a counter displaying the number of remaining trials.
Participants were instructed to choose between two cannon-ball containers, each associated with a reward probability that varied across the task.
A successful/rewarding choice would launch a burning cannonball towards a moving alien, awarding 100 points if it hit the target.
An unsuccessful choice would cause the cannonball to explode (-50 points), while a missed shot yielded 0 points (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: An unsuccessful choice would cause the cannonball to explode (-50 points), while a missed shot yielded 0 points (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: As such, learning which ball container had the greatest probability of success was necessary to perform well.
Participants were also required to aim at the alien, although this behaviour was only included as part of the cover story.
Crucially, reward probabilities changed throughout the task, with either the left or right container being most rewarding at any given time.
The frequency of the change in contingencies was a key manipulation here.
As in prior studies (Behrens et al., 2007; Browning et al., 2015), more frequent changes were used to create more volatile environments, while less frequent changes led to greater stability.
text.formatted: As in prior studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Behrens et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Browning et al., 2015)</ref>, more frequent changes were used to create more volatile environments, while less frequent changes led to greater stability.

text.text: Outcomes were complementary, such that a reward from the left container implied no reward from the right container and vice versa.
Each block of the task comprised 120 trials.
For volatile blocks, the reward probability associated with one of two cannons switched every 20 trials, while for stable blocks the reward probability switched every 60 trials (see Figure 2).
text.formatted: For volatile blocks, the reward probability associated with one of two cannons switched every 20 trials, while for stable blocks the reward probability switched every 60 trials (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: We crossed first-and second-block volatility factorially to disentangle effects of prior and current experience.
Participants completed only one task version to avoid carry-over effects between conditions.

Since we were interested in how learning rates generalise across distinct contexts, participants were presented with the message "You have now entered a new environment" before entering the second block, which had a visually distinct layout from the first block (see Figure 1), ensuring that participants perceived a significant change in the environmental context.
text.formatted: Since we were interested in how learning rates generalise across distinct contexts, participants were presented with the message "You have now entered a new environment" before entering the second block, which had a visually distinct layout from the first block (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>), ensuring that participants perceived a significant change in the environmental context.

text.text: The Rescorla-Wagner model is a classic, model-free reinforcement learning algorithm that characterises how agents update their beliefs (or expected values) based on prediction errors (Rescorla & Wagner, 1972).
text.formatted: The Rescorla-Wagner model is a classic, model-free reinforcement learning algorithm that characterises how agents update their beliefs (or expected values) based on prediction errors <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Rescorla & Wagner, 1972)</ref>.

text.text: The model maintains an expected value, 𝑉, for each option (choosing the left or right cannon), representing the agent's current belief about the likelihood of obtaining a given reward.

On each trial, after observing an outcome, this expected value is updated according to: where 𝑉 𝑡 is the expected value of a cannon before the current trial outcome is revealed, and 𝛿 𝑡 is the prediction error, defined as the difference between the observed outcomes (1=no explosion,0=explosion) and the current expectation:
The learning rate (𝛼), bounded between 0 and 1, determines the extent to which prediction errors update existing beliefs.
Value estimates were then transformed to choice probabilities via a softmax decision rule:
Where 𝜏 is a free parameter representing the decision temperature, which allows choices to vary from highly deterministic to highly stochastic.

Following prior studies, (Behrens et al., 2007; Browning et al., 2015) the key parameter of interest from this model was the learning rate (α), as it directly quantifies how quickly participants adjust their beliefs in response to new information and is expected to vary according to the statistics of the environment.

text.text: For instance, in volatile environments, where reward probabilities change frequently, adaptive behaviour is characterised by higher learning rates, whereas in stable environments, lower learning rates are more optimal for obtaining more reliable estimates (Behrens et al., 2007).

text.text: We estimated learning rates separately for each condition.

To improve parameter estimation, the computational models were embedded within a Hierarchical Bayesian model (Geen & Gerraty, 2021; Veenman et al., 2024) in which we assume that participant-level parameters are drawn from a single group-level distribution.

text.text: Learning rate estimates were then logit-transformed to convert the bounded [0, 1] values to a continuous scale.
Participants excluded from the task data were also removed from the questionnaire data to ensure consistency across analyses.
Those who showed inattentive responding through failed attention checks, embedded as single infrequency items within each questionnaire, were also excluded.
Specifically, if participants failed more than one infrequency item (where the 1 st and 2 nd most "correct" answers were accepted) they were not included in statistical analyses.
We also excluded any participant for whom full questionnaire data was not collected (due to a recording error) from these analyses.

To examine how learning styles generalised across environments with varying levels of uncertainty, a 2x2 between-subjects ANOVA was conducted using second-block learning rates as a function of current (stable vs. volatile) and previous (stable vs. volatile) block volatility.
Note that we discarded data from the first block for this analysis, as this is only to used establish prior volatility.
This allowed us to assess both how learning rates adapted to the current level of uncertainty and whether prior experience influenced belief updating in new environmental contexts.

To address whether trait anxiety or other mental health symptoms significantly influenced the extent to which learning styles generalised across environments, we conducted exploratory regression analyses.
Here, we extracted an index of adaptation or generalisation by calculating the difference between the learning rate in the first and second block of the task.
The interpretation of this metric differs according to the task version, but enables us to quantify the extent to which learning rates are stable across different blocks of the task.
We used regression models to establish the extent to which this measure was predicted by scores on the measures described previously, controlling for age and gender.
We entered each score into a separate regression model, and used false discovery rate (FDR) correction to correct for multiple comparisons across models.
We also included a sensitivity analysis where, rather than predicting difference scores, we predicted learning rate on the second block controlling for learning rate on the first block.
Given high correlations between the different questionnaire measures, we also used exploratory factor analysis to derive a low-dimensional representation of the data.
This was implemented in Python (via the Factor Analyzer package: https://factor-analyzer.readthedocs.io/) using maximum likelihood estimation and oblimin as the rotation method.

text.text: The resulting factors were entered into a single regression model predicting the difference in learning rate between blocks.
Our primary analyses focused on the learning rate parameter derived from a simple Rescorla-Wagner learning model, based on prior literature that had used a similar approach.

However, to provide a more parsimonious approach for quantifying effects of current and prior volatility on learning rate, we additionally built extended models that incorporated effects of these factors directly on model parameters.

Here, rather than separately fitting the computational model and then submitting its parameter estimates to a subsequent ANOVA, we jointly estimate parameters of the computational model itself and parameters determining the influence of environmental volatility.
These analyses were exploratory and did not form part of the pre-registered analysis plan.
We also evaluated alternative computational models.

First, we expanded the Rescorla-Wagner model to allow asymmetric updating of value estimates depending on prediction error valence in line with previous findings showing that participants do not learn equivalently from positive and negative prediction errors (Palminteri et al., 2017).
text.formatted: First, we expanded the Rescorla-Wagner model to allow asymmetric updating of value estimates depending on prediction error valence in line with previous findings showing that participants do not learn equivalently from positive and negative prediction errors <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Palminteri et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Here, the learning rate used on a given trial 𝛼 𝑡 depends upon the sign of the prediction error 𝛿 𝑡.
Both 𝛼 + and 𝛼 -are free parameters representing the learning rate for positive and negative prediction errors respectively.

We also evaluated a model using a Pearce-Hall update rule (Pearce & Hall, 1980) wherein the learning rate on the next trial 𝛼 𝑡+1 depends on the magnitude of recent prediction errors, allowing the learning rate to vary dynamically.
text.formatted: We also evaluated a model using a Pearce-Hall update rule <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Pearce & Hall, 1980)</ref> wherein the learning rate on the next trial 𝛼 𝑡+1 depends on the magnitude of recent prediction errors, allowing the learning rate to vary dynamically.

text.text: Specifically, the learning rate is updated based on the difference between the absolute prediction error |𝛿 𝑡 | and the previous learning rate 𝛼 𝑡 , with this update weighted according to an additional free parameter 𝛾.
As such, the learning rate increases when error is high and reduces when error is low, with the extent of these changes dependent upon 𝛾.
Finally, we also evaluated two approximately Bayesian learning models, referred to as leaky Beta models (Wise et al., 2019; Wise & Dolan, 2020; Sookud et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Finally, we also evaluated two approximately Bayesian learning models, referred to as leaky Beta models <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Wise et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Wise & Dolan, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Sookud et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These models maintain a probability distribution over the expected value of a choice, represented using a Beta distribution since expected value in this task is bounded between 0 and 1.
On each trial, the two parameters of the Beta distribution 𝐴 and 𝐵 are updated as follows:
Here, 𝜏 represents the extent to which a given outcome is allowed to update the current estimate; with higher values, recent outcomes have a greater impact.
A degree of forgetting is permitted by 𝜆 which decrements the current value of 𝐴 and 𝐵 on each trial.
We bound the value of these parameters at minimum value of 1 to provide a flat baseline distribution.
We can then calculate a point estimate of the expected value by taking the mean of this distribution:
We also implemented an asymmetric variant of this model, in which the 𝐴 and 𝐵 are updated at different rates, such that outcome valence determines the speed of updating:
This asymmetric updating is determined by two update parameters 𝜏 + and 𝜏 -which determine the update rate for positive and negative outcomes respectively.
As with the standard Rescorla-Wagner model, the expected value estimated by each of these models is transformed to choice probabilities using the softmax function described in Eq.
We implemented these models such that the group mean of each model parameter 𝜇 𝜃 was a linear function of the task conditions:
Where 𝑣 cur refers to the volatility of the current block and 𝑣 prev refers to the volatility of the previous block, with each coded as [-0.5, 0.5].
Each contributes to the parameter group mean to an extent governed by coefficients 𝛽 cur and 𝛽 prev , together with their interaction 𝛽 𝑖𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑟𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 ⋅ 𝑣 cur ⋅ 𝑣 prev and an intercept 𝜇.
This forms a hierarchical model with random intercepts but not random slopes; the between-subjects nature of our experimental design makes estimation of random slopes impossible.

As a result, this enables us to estimate the group-level effects of the task conditions on all model parameters in a similar way to our ANOVA analyses, but through a more parsimonious process that jointly estimates the computational model parameters.
Models were estimated using MCMC as described previously, and report model coefficients alongside equal tailed intervals as a measure of uncertainty in the estimated parameter values.
To aid interpretation, we report coefficients from the model on the untransformed learning rate scale.

Participants learn to select the optimal choice
We recruited a sample of 402 participants.
After exclusions based on data quality filters, we retained 330 participants (see Table S1 for exclusion reasons).
text.formatted: After exclusions based on data quality filters, we retained 330 participants (see Table <ref type="table">S1</ref> for exclusion reasons).

text.text: Due to a data recording issue, demographic information was only available for 302 of these participants (166 male, 136 female; Mean age=42.39, SD=11.94).

Participants performed well in the task, selecting the optimal choice (i.e., that most likely to lead to reward) on an average of 77% (SD=8.9%) of choices and receiving an average of 66.8% (SD=6.4%) rewarded outcomes across the task variants and across both blocks, indicating that they learned which option to select based on observed outcomes.

As expected, an ANOVA revealed that current block volatility (F(1, 326) = 10.04, p = .002, ηp² = .03) had a significant positive effect on learning rate derived from the Rescorla-Wagner learning model, such that learning rates were higher when participants were currently in a volatile environment.

However, and in line with our hypothesis, we also observed a significant effect of previous block volatility (F(1, 326) = 7.72, p = .006, ηp² = .02, Figure 3), indicating that learning rates were higher when participants had previously experienced a volatile environment.
text.formatted: However, and in line with our hypothesis, we also observed a significant effect of previous block volatility (F(1, 326) = 7.72, p = .006, ηp² = .02, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>), indicating that learning rates were higher when participants had previously experienced a volatile environment.

text.text: The interaction between current and previous block volatility was not significant (F(1, 326) = 3.70, p = .055, ηp² = .01), indicating that there was no clear evidence of a difference between stable and volatile current environments in the effect of previous volatility.

Follow-up t-tests also revealed that this effect was most prominent in the current volatile condition (t(160) = -3.81, corrected p < .001, d = 0.60), while no significant difference was found when comparing conditions where the current block was stable (t(166) = 0.57, corrected p = 1.00, d = 0.09).

Model comparison determined that the data was equally well explained by a dual learning rate Rescorla-Wagner model (ELPD_LOO = -13215.38, SE = 108.80) and an asymmetric leaky beta model (ELPD_LOO = -13185.90, SE = 107.85; Figure 4A), with stacking weights equal (w = .44 for both models; Figure 4B).

text.text: We opted to use the dual learning rate model for further analyses since it was simpler, having one less parameter, and consistent with prior literature using Rescorla-Wagner models for this task.

text.text: Adaptive learning requires appropriate use of prior knowledge about environmental statistics to guide present belief updating.
The present study investigates whether learning rates generalise across distinct environments and to what extent prior environmental experience influences subsequent belief updating.
The results provide evidence for a cross-environment carry-over effect that suggests that humans generalise perceptions of environmental statistics across distinct contexts.

Consistent with previous research, current volatility significantly increased learning rates, indicating that participants placed greater weight on recent outcomes when stimulus-outcome contingencies changed more frequently (Behrens et al., 2007; McGuire et al., 2014; Nassar et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Consistent with previous research, current volatility significantly increased learning rates, indicating that participants placed greater weight on recent outcomes when stimulus-outcome contingencies changed more frequently <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Behrens et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">McGuire et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Nassar et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: However, previous block volatility was also found to have a significant positive effect, indicating that prior exposure to a volatile environment was associated with higher subsequent learning rates.
This extends evidence suggesting that volatility-dependent learning strategies can generalise across environments.
For instance, Wen et al. (2023) found that prior exposure to high versus low volatility of task rule changes influenced learning rates in a subsequent mediumvolatility environment.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Wen et al. (2023)</ref> found that prior exposure to high versus low volatility of task rule changes influenced learning rates in a subsequent mediumvolatility environment.

text.text: The present findings extend this principle to reward-based belief updating across perceptually distinct environments.

These findings are consistent with accounts of human learning in which learners infer higherorder environmental statistics, including volatility, to regulate the weighting of prediction errors and distinguish meaningful changes in contingencies from stochastic fluctuations (Nassar et al., 2010; Piray & Daw, 2021).
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with accounts of human learning in which learners infer higherorder environmental statistics, including volatility, to regulate the weighting of prediction errors and distinguish meaningful changes in contingencies from stochastic fluctuations <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Nassar et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Piray & Daw, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Hierarchical Bayesian accounts similarly propose that inferred uncertainty and volatility continuously modulate updating via the precision-weighting of prediction errors (Mathys et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Hierarchical Bayesian accounts similarly propose that inferred uncertainty and volatility continuously modulate updating via the precision-weighting of prediction errors <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Mathys et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The significant effects of both current and previous volatility therefore suggest that learning rate calibration incorporates both immediate prediction errors from the current environment alongside information accumulated from prior experience.

The comparable effect of current relative to previous volatility indicates that current environmental demands exert a substantial influence on learning rate calibration, reinforcing the notion that prior experience provides an additive rather than deterministic influence on belief updating.

These findings also extend emerging accounts investigating meta-learning and generalisation of learning strategies. Simoens et al. (2024) showed that people can learn environment-specific reward learning rates and retrieve them when switching between previously experienced environments, while in a continuous estimation task Simoens et al. (2026) demonstrated both rapid within-block adaptation alongside slower, environment-specific learning rate adjustments reflecting accumulated experience.
text.formatted: These findings also extend emerging accounts investigating meta-learning and generalisation of learning strategies. <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Simoens et al. (2024)</ref> showed that people can learn environment-specific reward learning rates and retrieve them when switching between previously experienced environments, while in a continuous estimation task <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Simoens et al. (2026)</ref> demonstrated both rapid within-block adaptation alongside slower, environment-specific learning rate adjustments reflecting accumulated experience.

text.text: In the present task, this influence occurred across a transition between two temporally separate and visually distinct environments rather than through revisiting an identical environment, indicating that knowledge about environmental statistics survives transitions between environments.

More generally, this is in line with a heuristics account of decision-making (Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier, 2011), in that rather than reflecting complete transfer, meta-generalisation may reflect a subconscious trade-off between reusing previously acquired knowledge and the flexibility required to adapt to the current environmental statistics (Verbeke et al., 2025; Holton et al., 2025).
text.formatted: More generally, this is in line with a heuristics account of decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier, 2011)</ref>, in that rather than reflecting complete transfer, meta-generalisation may reflect a subconscious trade-off between reusing previously acquired knowledge and the flexibility required to adapt to the current environmental statistics <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Verbeke et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Holton et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: When estimating different learning rates for positive and negative prediction errors, both learning rates were equally influenced by volatility, suggesting a general shift in the rate of belief updating than a valence-specific change in learning.

This distinction is relevant given that previous evidence has identified asymmetric updating of positive and negative information in anxiety and depression, including differences in how desirable and undesirable outcomes influence belief updating (Gagne et al., 2022; Pulcu & Browning, 2017; Solovey et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This distinction is relevant given that previous evidence has identified asymmetric updating of positive and negative information in anxiety and depression, including differences in how desirable and undesirable outcomes influence belief updating <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Gagne et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Pulcu & Browning, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Solovey et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Contrary to our predictions for the exploratory individual difference analyses, trait anxiety and other mental health measures did not significantly predict learning rate changes.

These null findings contrast with evidence linking anxiety-related traits to altered uncertainty estimation, volatility adaptation, and belief updating (Browning et al., 2015; Gibbs-Dean et al., 2023; McCoy & Lawson, 2025; Hein et al., 2021; Pulcu & Browning, 2019), as well as evidence that trait anxiety can alter generalisation of learned values between stimuli (Verra et al., 2025).
text.formatted: These null findings contrast with evidence linking anxiety-related traits to altered uncertainty estimation, volatility adaptation, and belief updating <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Browning et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Gibbs-Dean et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">McCoy & Lawson, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Hein et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Pulcu & Browning, 2019)</ref>, as well as evidence that trait anxiety can alter generalisation of learned values between stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Verra et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, these findings should be interpreted with caution since the sample size here is relatively small compared to prior studies and may be underpowered given the typical effect sizes observed in these studies.
Despite these compelling findings, several limitations that constrain mechanistic interpretations should be acknowledged.
First, our results say little about the factors governing the generalisation of learning rate.
For example, generalisation is known to follow a gradient according to relevant features (Shepard, 1987), and this was untested in this study.
text.formatted: For example, generalisation is known to follow a gradient according to relevant features <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Shepard, 1987)</ref>, and this was untested in this study.

text.text: Future work could manipulate similarity between environments to establish the boundaries on generalisation.
Second, contexts are often not so clearly demarcated in the real world.

Humans are adept at inferring latent states of the world in the absence of obvious boundary markers (Nguyen et al., 2026; Mirea et al., 2024), and future work could examine how contexts are detected, separated, and categorised based purely on their environmental statistics in order to facilitate generalisation of learning.
text.formatted: Humans are adept at inferring latent states of the world in the absence of obvious boundary markers <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Nguyen et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Mirea et al., 2024)</ref>, and future work could examine how contexts are detected, separated, and categorised based purely on their environmental statistics in order to facilitate generalisation of learning.

text.text: In conclusion, the findings from the present study provide evidence for cross-environment carryover effects of reward-based learning rate adaptation.

These findings support a meta-learning account of adaptive learning in which prior environmental experience can shape how rapidly beliefs are updated, while learning remains responsive to the statistics of the current environment.

All code underwent human review.
Figure 1.
A visual schematic of the cannonball task.
Participants learned to update and optimise their decisions through trial-and-error learning, without explicit knowledge of the underlying task structure.

This model-free reinforcement learning task captures learning styles by quantifying participants' choice behaviour (switching between the left and right cannon) as they update their expectations based on prior reward outcomes (i.e., the cannonball explodes or fires).
Figure 2.
Generating choice-reward contingencies.
A) Probability of explosion for the right cannon (left cannon used the inverse probability) in the stable blocks.
B) Probability of explosion for the right cannon in the volatile blocks.
C) Task structure.
Each participant completed one of four versions, each providing a unique combination of stable and volatile conditions across the two blocks.
Figure 3.
Learning rates across different task conditions.
Learning rates derived from the Rescorla-Wagner learning model are shown across the four combinations of previous and current volatility.

Black points represent group means, error bars represent 95% confidence intervals around this mean, and coloured points represent individual subject learning rates. *** = p < .001, n.s. = not significant.
text.formatted: Black points represent group means, error bars represent 95% confidence intervals around this mean, and coloured points represent individual subject learning rates. *** = p < .001, n.s. = not significant.

text.text: Figure 4.
Extended model comparison results.

A) Expected log pointwise density (ELPD) values relative to the bestscoring model (asymmetric leaky beta) for each candidate model, demonstrating that the dual learning rate Rescorla-Wagner model and asymmetric leaky beta models performed substantially better than alternative models, but were themselves tied.
Error bars represent the standard error.
B) Stacking weights for each candidate model, showing that weight was shared equally between the dual learning rate Rescorla-Wagner and asymmetric leaky beta models.
C)
Figure 5.
Effects of current and previous volatility in the extended dual learning rate Rescorla-Wagner model.
A) Positive learning rates from the model across the four experimental conditions.

Black points represent the posterior mean of the group-level learning rate in each condition, error bars represent the 95% equal tailed interval, and the coloured points represent individual participants' posterior mean estimates.
B) Effects of current and previous block volatility, alongside their interaction, on positive learning rate within the model.
Points represent the mean of the posterior distribution from the Bayesian model while error bars represent the 95% equal tailed interval.
C) Negative learning rates from the model across the four conditions.
D) Effects of current and previous block volatility, alongside their interaction, on negative learning rates.
